Before you start

Slide 2 · Notes

Read each one; hands go up and down quickly. Point out that most hands went up: this is all of us. Don’t ask for stories.

Slide 3 · Notes

The threat system spots an insult and readies your body before you’ve thought it through. The brakes in the prefrontal cortex read context and catch up later; they keep maturing into your mid-20s. Ask: what makes your fuse shorter?

Slide 4 · Notes

Thumbs up, down or sideways. Next slide shows the answer.

Slide 5 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 6 · Notes

Exercise is great for you. It just isn’t the best tool while you’re boiling. A run later in the day is different.

Slide 7 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 8 · Notes

Catch it: jaw, shoulders, heat, typing faster. Bring it down: in for 4, out for 6, cold water, a slow walk. Zoom out. Then decide once you’re at a 3 or 4: what line got crossed, and is it worth raising? The out-loud time-out: “I’m too heated to talk well. Give me 20 minutes.” Then come back.

Slide 9 · Notes

People who replayed an angering memory from across the room felt less angry than people who relived it from the inside.

Slide 10 · Notes

Two minutes. No real blowups or names.

Slide 11 · Notes

Take a few. The earlier you catch it, the more options you have.

Slide 12 · Notes

Quitting by text now is the heat talking, and her family may count on the paycheck. Saying nothing lets it happen again.

Slide 13 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 14 · Notes

His anger is right about the problem. Posting later and tagging the classmate usually makes it bigger.

Private. Nobody shares. Offer a second question for early finishers: what are the anger rules in your family, and which do you want to keep? Choosing when to speak is a skill.

Two minutes in pairs. Nobody speaks for a group, and no personal stories.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why anger moves faster than judgment (a fast alarm, slower brakes), why venting tends to feed anger, and how to handle anger in order: let the energy drop, then use the information. Each student leaves with one move they'd like to try. Nobody has to share a real blowup.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 2 minSound familiar?
  2. 2 minA fast alarm, and slower brakes
  3. 3 minThe punching bag, and what brings it down
  4. 3 minThe core skill, and the fly on the wall
  5. 3 minYour first sign: turn and talk, share out
  6. 5 minThree situations: Ines, Noah, Sam
  7. 2 minWhat was underneath, close

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

The punching bag vote, the core skill, one of the three situations, and one move.

Before you teach
Keep it off real people in the room.

Anger talk can slide into naming a teacher, a teammate or a sibling. Steer back gently: "Let's keep names out of it. What would help in a moment like that?" The scenarios are there so nobody has to use their own story.

Nobody shares their own blowup.

The reflection card is private and goes home with the student. Passing is always fine in the circle.

If someone else's anger feels unsafe.

If a student says anger at home, in a relationship or at school makes them feel unsafe, thank them, don't dig for details in the group, and connect them with a counselor that day. The student page says plainly that this isn't theirs to handle alone.

If a student has hurt someone or themselves when angry.

That's a counselor conversation, not a discussion topic. Don't ask screening questions in advisory. Walk them over or let the counselor know after.

Who gets read as angry is a real topic.

Some students, often Black students and students of color, have been called aggressive when they were being firm. If it comes up, believe them and name it as unfair. Don't ask anyone to prove it or explain it for the group.

Model the skill you're teaching.

If the room gets heated, you can say it out loud: "I'm going to slow this down for a second." Students learn the time-out from watching an adult use one.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Race and who gets called aggressive.

The Hugenberg study is on the slide on purpose. Present it as bias in the people watching, and keep the focus on what a student can do if they've been misread: talk it through with someone they trust. Avoid using any student's experience as the example.

Family anger rules differ.

In some homes raised voices blow over in minutes. In others, anger at an elder crosses a serious line. Present both as normal, avoid "In X families" generalizations, and keep the family-rules question private. Say "parent or caregiver": Sam's scenario uses a grandmother.

Girls get angry. Boys get hurt.

Students hear early on that anger is unattractive in girls and that boys should only show anger. Mix genders in your examples, and when naming what's under anger, say clearly that anyone can be hurt, scared or embarrassed.

Bodies and brains signal differently.

Some students, including autistic students and students with ADHD, notice body signals late, or get flooded by noise, crowds or sensory overload before anger shows. "Catch it early" can mean noticing the room, too. Don't treat eye contact or staying seated as signs of calm, and never use "psycho" or "crazy" as shorthand.

Not everyone can walk away.

Ines may not be able to quit a job her family counts on, and some students can't leave a room at work or at home. Breathing out slowly and cold water on the hands work anywhere and cost nothing. Name those first.

Faith can be a tool.

For some students, prayer, a verse or a moment of quiet is how they cool down. For others it's music or a walk. "Whatever brings your body down" covers all of it.

What the research says

Neuroscientist James Blair calls the amygdala, hypothalamus and periaqueductal gray the brain's "basic threat system" and links it to both anger and reactive aggression. The prefrontal cortex reads context and can turn the alarm down.

Blair, 2012, WIREs Cognitive Science

Angry college students who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who angered them ended up angrier and more aggressive than students who did nothing at all.

Bushman, 2002, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

A review of 154 studies found that activities that lower arousal (slow breathing, muscle relaxation, mindfulness, slow yoga, a time-out) reduced anger. Activities that raise it, like running or boxing, generally did not, and sometimes made it worse.

Kjærvik and Bushman, 2024, Clinical Psychology Review

People who looked back on an angering memory from a "fly on the wall" view felt less angry than people who relived it from the inside.

Kross, Ayduk and Mischel, 2005, Psychological Science

White participants with more implicit racial bias were quicker to see anger in Black faces than in white faces.

Hugenberg and Bodenhausen, 2003, Psychological Science

People who suppressed their emotions during a conversation came across as less responsive, and their partners formed more negative impressions. The cost was smaller for people with more Asian cultural values, where restraint is expected.

Butler, Lee and Gross, 2007, Emotion
